Senses.Explanation: Literally "outside the eon." The Chan corpus uses it as a productive modifier and location in sayings and verse: "spring light beyond the eon" (劫外春光), "the spring beyond the eon returns and the ten thousand things wither" (劫外春回萬物枯), and "the true lineage beyond the eon" (劫外真宗). It is paired explicitly with the time before buddhas and patriarchs were born: "before buddhas and patriarchs were born, outside the empty eon" (佛祖未生空劫外). It also enters public address as a demand to "take responsibility beyond the eon" (於劫外承當), contrasted in the same question with meeting now (而今相見, "meeting at present"). The corpus thus bends chronological language into a recurrent Chan register for the sayings, activity, spring, and lineage it places outside or before measured epochs.
Senses.Note: Count: 740 occurrences in 221 allowlisted texts. Title uses such as "Record Beyond the Eon" (劫外錄) are proper-title compounds but do not make "beyond the eon" (劫外) itself a different thing. Related "empty eon" (空劫) should be cross-checked as a distinct headword, not silently equated.

Occurrences.Kwic: 儻肯於劫外承當，更何必而今相見？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A case commentary contrasts taking responsibility beyond the eon with meeting now.

Occurrences.Kwic: 壺中消息。劫外春光。還他一氣連枝。須是同身共命。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi's upper-hall record uses the recurrent spring-light compound.

Occurrences.Kwic: 佛祖未生空劫外，正偏不落有無機。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later upper-hall verse explicitly connects the phrase with before buddhas and patriarchs were born.

Occurrences.Kwic: 劫外春回萬物枯，山河大地一塵無。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public exchange answers with the verse line 'spring beyond the eon returns; all things wither.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 克揚劫外真宗，維暢今時懿矩。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A transmission-oriented prose passage calls it the true lineage beyond the eon and pairs it with present-day standards.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to eat gruel. The phrase occurs 748 times in 182 allowlisted texts. The records retain the concrete monastic meal: one early encounter describes five or six hundred people gathered to eat gruel and rice, and a later discourse lists spreading out the bowl, eating gruel, sleeping afterward, drinking tea, meeting guests, and eating rice at the midday meal. Zen deployment also puts this ordinary action into public answers. Asked what the non-teaching is, a master answers, ‘eat gruel and eat rice’; asked to indicate an entrance, another gives the same answer. A monk says that he saw a master ‘at the place of eating gruel and rice,’ after which the questioner points to the fire tongs and asks about that. Another record enumerates investigating Chan, eating gruel and rice, defecating and urinating, walking, sitting, and sleeping as ‘your own fundamental matter.’ The gruel is still food; the corpus-specific bend is that masters repeatedly make eating it an answer, an instruction, and an item in such enumerations rather than reserving it for meal notices.
Senses.Note: The corpus supplies no different referent or word class requiring a second sense: literal meal reports and interview answers both name the same act of eating gruel. Do not duplicate the fixed Zhaozhou question here; ‘have you eaten your gruel?’ has its own entry and is linked below. Family cross-check: this definition remains compatible with gruel, gruel and rice, the bowl, wash the bowl, and Zhaozhou’s fixed question; robe-and-bowl as a succession token is a different family deployment.

Occurrences.Kwic: 好五六百人聚頭，喫粥喫飯，為復見處一般，見處別？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Anthology of the Patriarchal Hall records a community of five or six hundred gathered to eat gruel and rice, then asks whether their places of seeing are alike or different.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問法尚應捨何況非法如何是非法師云喫粥喫飯
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a public exchange, the answer to ‘what is the non-teaching?’ is ‘eat gruel and eat rice.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 問乞師指箇入路師云喫粥喫飯
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A request to indicate an entrance receives ‘eat gruel and eat rice’ as the complete answer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 堂內展鉢喫粥，粥後打睡，睡起喫茶，見客相喚，齋時喫飯，日日相似，有甚麼過？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse places eating gruel in the concrete daily sequence of opening the bowl, sleeping, drinking tea, meeting guests, and eating the midday meal.

Occurrences.Kwic: 遇曰。什麼處見。對曰。喫粥喫飯處見。遇插火筯於爐中云。者箇又作麼生。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk says he saw the master ‘at the place of eating gruel and rice’; the interviewer then points to the fire tongs and asks about them.

Occurrences.Kwic: 參禪學道是汝本分事、喫粥喫飯是汝本分事、屙屎撒尿是汝本分事、行坐打眠是汝本分事
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse explicitly enumerates investigating Chan, eating gruel and rice, defecating and urinating, and walking, sitting, and sleeping as ‘your own fundamental matter.’

AlternateTargets: have you had your gruel yet?
Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘have you eaten your gruel yet?’ The exact question occurs 101 times in 67 allowlisted texts. It is the fixed opening reply in Zhaozhou’s wash-your-bowl case: a newly arrived monk asks for instruction; Zhaozhou asks whether he has eaten his gruel; when the monk says that he has, Zhaozhou says, ‘go wash your bowl.’ The record says that the monk awakened at the words. Later masters preserve the speaker turns and publicly examine them. Yunmen asks whether there was an instruction and, if not, why the monk awakened. Dahui repeats the case and reports that many places had raised it and added comments; elsewhere a verse begins with the question, names Zhaozhou, and continues with the command to wash the bowl. The question also recurs outside the copied case: asked ‘what is the student’s own self?’, a master replies with it and follows the student’s answer with ‘go wash your bowl.’ One later discourse reverses the received praise, calling ‘gruel eaten’ adding a head atop a head and ‘go wash the bowl’ drawing legs on a snake. Zen usage therefore bends an ordinary breakfast question into a recognizable public-case line whose recorded answer and later examinations travel with it.
Senses.Note: This is one fixed question and one corpus-wide case formula, not a master-specific sense: Zhaozhou supplies the named case, while later masters quote, verse, reuse, and criticize it. The direct question and its reuse still ask about the same completed meal, so item 8 does not license multiple senses. Distinguish the lexicalized question from the general phrase ‘eat gruel’ (喫粥); the two entries cross-reference rather than repeat definitions.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問趙州。學人乍入叢林。乞師指示。州云。爾喫粥了也未。僧云。喫粥了。州云。洗鉢盂去。僧忽然大悟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui’s record preserves the complete case sequence: the newcomer requests instruction, Zhaozhou asks the fixed question, the monk answers, Zhaozhou tells him to wash the bowl, and the record says the monk suddenly awakened.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問如何是學人自己師云喫粥了也未云喫粥也師云洗鉢盂去
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The question is redeployed as the answer to ‘what is the student’s own self?’ and retains the bowl-washing follow-up.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云且道有指示無指示若道有指示向他道什麼若道無指示者僧何得悟去
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Immediately after raising Zhaozhou’s case, the section’s master asks whether there was an instruction and, if not, why the monk awakened; the local speaker identity was not independently established, so it is left null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云。諸方拈掇甚多。下注脚亦不少。未曾有一人分明說破。妙喜今日為諸人分明說破。喫粥了便洗鉢盂。且道。還曾指示無。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui says many places have raised the case and added comments, restates ‘when the gruel is eaten, wash the bowl,’ and asks whether any instruction was given.

Occurrences.Kwic: 喫粥了也未。趙州無忌諱。更令洗鉢盂。太殺沒巴鼻。悟去由來不丈夫
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later verse opens with the fixed question, explicitly names Zhaozhou, and continues with the command to wash the bowl and an appraisal of the awakening.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂：喫粥了也，頭上安頭。洗鉢盂去，為虵畫足。更問如何日納敗闕？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later hall discourse gives an adverse appraisal: ‘gruel eaten’ is adding a head atop a head, and ‘go wash the bowl’ is drawing legs on a snake.

Senses.Explanation: The graphs mean “drink,” “tea,” and “go”: “go drink tea.” In Zhaozhou Congshen's recorded sayings, he asks one of two newly arrived monks whether he has been there before. The monk says no, and Zhaozhou tells him to go drink tea. The other says yes and receives the same words. When the temple steward asks why both received the same instruction, Zhaozhou calls “Steward!”; after the steward answers, Zhaozhou again says, “Go drink tea.” Five Lamps Compendium preserves the same exchange but reverses the order of the two monks. Elsewhere a master answers a question about “three-by-three in front and three-by-three behind” by asking the monk's name and then saying, “Go drink tea.” The saying also becomes the named allusion “Zhaozhou's tea,” often paired with “Yunmen's flatbread.” The headword occurs 781 times across 170 allowlisted texts; the spelling variant using the alternate graph for “drink” occurs 14 times across 7 texts. The records give no gloss beyond the literal wording.
Senses.Note: The originating exchange has multiple speakers, so its occurrence attribution remains null even though the case is Zhaozhou's. The witnesses differ in whether the monk who had or had not visited appears first. The steward's question preserves the point that both answers receive the same words. A later retelling uses the alternate graph for “drink.” Compare “Zhaozhou's tea,” “wash your bowl,” and “the ordinary mind.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 師問二新到上座曾到此間否云不曾到師云喫茶去又問那一人曾到此間否云曾到師云喫茶去
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Old Recorded Sayings of Venerable Masters, Zhaozhou's recorded sayings: the originating exchange and the steward's follow-up. It has multiple speakers, so the speaker field is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師問新到。曾到此間麼。曰。曾到。師曰。喫茶去。又問僧。僧曰。不曾到。師曰。喫茶去。後院主問曰。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Compendium, Zhaozhou's section: an independent witness of the originating exchange, with the two monks in the reverse order. It has multiple speakers.

Occurrences.Kwic: 昔趙州住院，有僧參次，州云：『上座曾到這裡麼？』僧云：『不曾到。』州云：『吃茶去。』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A retelling of Zhaozhou's exchange using the alternate graph for “drink”; the steward asks why both the visitor and nonvisitor are sent for tea.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問古人道前三三後三三意如何。師曰。汝名什麼。曰某甲。師曰。喫茶去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Jingde-era Record of the Transmission of the Lamp, section on Zifu Zhensui of Jizhou: another master answers an unrelated question with “go drink tea.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 一切法無差，雲門胡餅趙州茶。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An upper-hall verse pairs the established allusion “Zhaozhou's tea” with “Yunmen's flatbread.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 州曰：喫茶去。院主問：和尚為甚曾到也喫茶去，不曾到也喫茶去？州喚院主，主應諾。州曰：喫茶去。保福展云：趙州慣得其便。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Zhaozhou exchange is raised for later comments by Baofu Congzhan and Jingqing. The combination of case and commentary has multiple speakers.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘strike or clap the palms.’ The gesture occurs 746 times in 231 allowlisted texts, commonly as a visible turn in a public exchange. It may stand alone (‘clapped three times’), accompany departure, a shout, or a blow, or join laughter: ‘clapped his hands and laughed loudly’ occurs 98 times in 60 texts. The record does not assign one fixed attitude to it. One master claps and laughs before saying an answer is ‘not worth half a cent’; another monk claps once after shouting; Xiyuan claps three times when asked why he bathes without an attendant. Caoshan later explicitly calls the action ‘hand-clapping’ and distinguishes Xiyuan’s use from the same physical action elsewhere. In the Shuilao case, Shuilao rises after Mazu kicks him, claps and laughs, and speaks; later records repeatedly cite that sequence. Zen bends an ordinary gesture by making it an answer, rejoinder, appraisal, or recorded public-interview move, while the surrounding words—not the gesture alone—establish whether a given occurrence is laughter, challenge, celebration, or dismissal.
Senses.Note: Family check: “clap the hands” (撫掌), “hand-clapping” (拍手撫掌), “clap and laugh loudly” (撫掌大笑), “clap once” (撫掌一下), and “clap three times” (撫掌三下) all denote the same physical action. They differ in accompanying speech and count, not referent, so they remain one sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 乃撫掌作舞，大笑云：「菩薩子喫飯來！」後有僧舉問長慶：「古人撫掌大笑，意作摩生？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The action accompanies dancing, laughter, and a call to eat; a later monk asks about it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：和尚不使沙彌童行，何得自燒？師撫掌三下。後僧舉似曹山，山云：一等是箇拍手撫掌，就中西園奇怪，俱胝一指頭禪，蓋謂承當處不諦當。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xiyuan answers with three claps; Caoshan explicitly identifies the movement as hand-clapping.

Occurrences.Kwic: 主指曰：春雨霖霖。師撫掌大笑曰：不直半分錢。主便喝，師曰：者瞎漢向道不直半分錢，又惡發作什麼？主撫掌一下，師曰：且坐喫茶。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Two speakers clap at different turns in a public exchange; one clap accompanies a stated appraisal.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大師欄胷與一踏踏倒，當下大悟，起來撫掌大笑云：也大奇！也大奇！百千法門，無量妙義，只向一毫頭上識得根源去。便作禮。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Shuilao case preserves the sequence kick, rise, clap, laugh, speak, and bow.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧以手面前一劃師云是何言欵僧便喝師云作甚麼僧撫掌一下便打師云瞎漢乱做作麼以坐具真打出法堂
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk claps once and strikes during an exchange, showing the gesture outside laughter.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂撫掌大笑良久曰大眾笑箇什麼山僧笑古往今來一切人有瞥地有不瞥地
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teaching-seat occurrence begins with prolonged clapping and laughter and then explicitly asks what is being laughed at.

Senses.Explanation: An imperative: do not (莫) understand or take it (會) wrongly (錯). Its distinct Chan deployment is as a master's warning attached directly to a saying or answer in public discourse. Asked the intention of the coming from the West, one master answers 'it is so, but do not get it wrong.' An extended address says not to infer 'not round and not sudden' from the preceding words and not to present borrowed, similar, or calculated phrases as one's own understanding, repeating 'do not get it wrong.' Elsewhere a master warns an assembly not to say that speech, silence, movement, and stillness are all buddha-affairs. The formula can also follow an unexplained seasonal statement — 'yesterday snow, today it melts' — leaving the warning itself as the only explicit appraisal. These contexts establish the public-interview function without supplying an interpretation of what the preceding words secretly mean.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 168 hits in 73 texts. Variants include emphatic take care not to get it wrong (莫錯會好) and just do not get it wrong (且莫錯會). One imperative sense; preceding statements do not create different referents.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問。如何是西來意。師曰。是即是。莫錯會。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Public interview: the warning is attached to an answer about the west-coming intention.

Occurrences.Kwic: 莫錯會好莫見與麼道便向不圓不頓處卜度者裏也須是箇人始得莫將依師語相似語測度語到處呈中將為自己見解莫錯會
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The text specifies several wrong receptions: inference, borrowed phrases, and calculated phrases presented as one's own.

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸人還委悉麼？莫道語默動靜無非佛事好，且莫錯會。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Assembly warning against a stated generalization about speech, silence, movement, and stillness.

Occurrences.Kwic: 昨日雪，今日消。仔細高著眼，莫錯會好！
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hall-address use after an ordinary seasonal statement, without an explanatory gloss.
